data.title: Baptismal Memrā’ of Anonymous Author of the Ninth Century
data.abstractNote: “Exposition of the Church Services” (ECS) is a 9th century liturgical commentary, the first and integral liturgical work about the East Syrian liturgy after the great liturgical reformation of Patriarch Išo’yahb III. Though the Author of the ECS comments on the various memrē of the Church of the East, we shall pay attention mainly to the baptismal memrā, which is the most remarkable among the memrē commented on by the Author. At first, we shall discuss the different terms and methods of baptism together with the manuscripts and editions of East Syrian baptismal liturgy. The baptismal memrā contains nine chapters and an analysis of the content of each chapter provides us with a clear outlook about the content of the text. The Author highlights the Pauline theology that explains baptism as a participation in the death and resurrection of Christ. The Author speaks about three anointings upon the candidate: pre-baptismal rušmā, anointing of the whole body and the post-baptismal rušmā. He emphasizes the pouring out of the consecrated water before the post-baptismal rušmā. He sets the baptismal rite within the framework of Eucharistic celebration, and the reception of the Eucharist by the baptized is presupposed in the commentary. A lucid idea is depicted in the commentary about the rights and duties of the sponsors too. In short, the baptismal commentary of the Anonymous Author of the 9th century provides us with a holistic view about the East Syrian rite of baptism.

data.title: Jacques Rhétoré. La versification en Soureth (araméen contemporain)
data.abstractNote:
Alessandro Mengozzi
Published Online: 2017-11-14 | DOI: https://doi.org/10.1515/olzg-2017-0117
Licensed Access
Download PDF

Bruno Poizat, former professor of mathematics at the University of Lyon, traveler in the Middle East, fluent speaker of Neo-Aramaic as a foreign language and teacher of Sureth at INALCO, publishes in this book a manuscript by Jacques Rhétoré that he found some years ago in the archives of the Dominicans of Saulchoir (Paris) and an updated catalogue of modern critical editions and manuscript collections of Sureth texts. In the convenient form of a volume of the Subsidia series, he thus adds a precious source of data, information and critical reflection to the two anthologies of Sureth religious poems published in the series Scriptores Syri of CSCO, voll. 589–90 and 627–8.

The first part of the volume (pp. 1–77) is an accurate edition of the uncompleted and so far unpublished work La versification en Soureth by French Dominican Jacques Rhétoré (1841–1921). The second part (79–141) contains most valuable information on Sureth literature, with updated bibliography, and a detailed and very informative commentary on Rhétoré‘s text by the editor.

A missionary from 1874 in Mosul and in the mountainous region between Van and Mosul, Rhétoré wrote grammars of Armenian and two varieties of Neo-Aramaic: Ṭūrōyo – also called Ṣūrayt, a cluster of Neo-Aramaic dialects spoken in Ṭūr ʻAbdīn, south-eastern Turkey – and Sureth, an autoglottonym used, among other names – (Modern) Aramaic, Assyrian, (Modern) Syriac, Vernacular Syriac–, for North-Eastern Neo-Aramaic varieties that were and are spoken and occasionally written by Christians of various denominations–especially Assyrians, Chaldeans and Syrian Catholics – in northern Iraq, south-eastern Turkey, Syria and north-western Iran.

Father Rhétoré collected and studied manuscripts of Sureth religious poems and in the second part of the volume Poizat gives a detailed description (95–9) of ten items that are now kept in the library of the Dominicans of Mosul, recently rescued from IS violence by their heroic Superior, Father Michaeel Najeeb. In continuity of ideas with Rhétoré, Father Najeeb has spent and is spending much time and energies in a project of digitization of books and manuscripts belonging to the Iraqi Dominicans and to other private and public Christian libraries of the plain of Mosul. In 2014, he moved the library of the Dominican Friars of Mosul (DFM) from Qaraqosh to Erbil. A provisional description of the manuscripts of this collection is now available in the online database of the Hill Museum & Manuscript Library (HMML) at Saint John's Abbey and University in Collegeville, Minnesota (www.hmml.org).

Rhétoré realized the cultural importance of the traditional stanzaic poems among the Aramaic-speaking Christians and their potential as pastoral tools for the Catholic missionaries, who in the 19th century were particularly active and successful in bringing the native Christians of the plain of Mosul to union with Rome and what they held as orthodox theology. They also introduced devotional practices of contemporary European Catholicism in northern Iraq.

In this work – that Poizat faithfully reproduces in print, including the author's erasures, corrections, old-fashioned spellings and secondary additions–, Father Rhétoré shows he is aware of the social function of poetry among native Syrians: poetry serves for liturgical and pedagogical purposes and it is required on certain special occasions in their public life. He therefore writes this ars poetica as a tutorial for missionaries, who may themselves compose verses, precisely as he did. Indeed, with the pseudonym Yaqo Nukhraya (Jacques l'Étranger) or Yaqo bar Qushta (Jacques le Véridique), Rhétoré composed fables in verse, songs and hymns, sometimes with the assistance of the famous native poet and bard David the Blind. On the basis of the HMML database, a number of Sureth works by Rhétoré can be added to Poizat's list (84–6): the translation of a number of books associated with devotional practices, dated 1877 (Confraternitas SS. Nominis Jesu, DFM 95; Militiae Angelicae seu cinguli Sancti Thomae Aquinatis, DFM 96; Via Crucis, DFM 344); The Life of St. Blaise, Martyr and Bishop of Sebaste, in prose (DFM 132, 1879); and the bilingual – French and Sureth – La Montagnarde Chaldéenne et l'Ange, “on the social, political, religious, and moral situation of the Church of the East”, with notes (DFM 346).

La Versification en Soureth is divided into a prologue and ten chapters. The first (Notions générales sur la poësie soureth) and ninth (Défauts et qualités des versificateurs soureth) chapters are more critical in nature and reveal Rhétoré's attitude towards Sureth poetry and the society of which it is a typical cultural expression. According to Rhétoré, despite their religious inspiration and their roots in late Classical Syriac hymnography, Sureth poems represent a simple and primitive form of folk poetry, which is cultivated by and for uneducated, often illiterate, peasants and herders. Rhétoré recognizes the oral context in which Sureth poems were produced and transmitted, the subordination of metrics to music, the circulation and success of texts thanks to roaming bards like David the Blind, Thomas Sindjari, and Elias of Tchamba, who travelled from village to village to sing fables, songs and hymns and collect food and money for their families. Nevertheless, as a 19th–century scholar, he is not methodologically equipped to appreciate the aesthetics of repetition and rhythm and the formulaic features of oral literature in the vernacular, while he criticizes the abuse of poetic license and of Arabic and Kurdish words, the prolixity and bad taste of Sureth poets.

Chapters 2 to 7 are more technical in nature: they explain and exemplify the structure of feet, rhymes (the manuscript DFM 235 preserves a list of rhyming words by Rhétoré), caesurae and stanzas. The eighth chapter is an anthology of excerpts of various genres and meters, while the ninth chapter is a gold mine of bio-bibliographical information on Sureth poets whose lives and works would otherwise be barely known. Among other additions and up-dating, Poizat's notes help identify the manuscript sources and provide a French translation of the excerpts included by Rhétoré in his anthology, adding precious bibliographical and factual information on Sureth poets.

data.title: Nota et familiaria castra: Soldier and Civilian in Roman Syria and Mesopotamia
data.abstractNote:
This dissertation is a study of the political, social and economic interaction of soldiers and civilians in Roman Syria and Mesopotamia from the reign of Augustus to the Arab Conquest.
Part One examines the interrelationship of urbanism and the Roman army, using archaeological and epigraphic evidence, in particular looking at the phenomenon of army units based in or near cities in the Principate, and the development of fortress cities in the later empire.
Part Two is a study of the political, social and cultural interaction of soldiers and civilians, examining the army as an agency of control, and issues such as the ethnic and cultural identities of soldiers.
Part Three is a study of the role of the army in the regional economy of Syria and Mesopotamia, looking at the interrelationship of taxation, army pay, army supply, production and trade.
The general theme of the study is that despite the physical proximity of large concentrations of soldiers and civilians there was greater social and cultural separation than one might expect from a superficial examination of the evidence, and that the army was primarily an agency of control and exploitation of the provinces rather than a factor in their development.

data.title: About Naked Women and Adam’s Body: The Syriac-Christian Cave of Treasures as a Source of Islamic Storytelling
data.abstractNote: The motif of the descent of the “sons of God” to the daughters of men was liberated from its hybrid connotations indicating a mixture between the divine and the human, once it was instead interpreted to mean that the sons of Seth had descended towards the daughters of Cain. The influence of this theme in Syriac Christianity upon Islamic authors is worth considering, documenting as it does a direct contact between the two religions. In addition, the related topic of Adam’s body being taken out of Paradise into the Ark constitutes a fruitful theme for interreligious narrative transformations. Especially noteworthy is the designation of Adam’s body as bema, which can be connected to Syriac liturgical usage for the separation between men and women in the church. This may shed new light upon similar regulations in the synagogue.

data.title: Yūḥannā Ibn Sarābiyūn: Further Studies Into the Transmission of His Works
data.abstractNote: Ibn Sarabiyun is one of the last exponents of classical Syriac medical writing, and one of the most influential authors for the development of medical theory and practice in late ninth-century Baghdad in particular, and for the Arabic medical tradition in general. During the last thirty years, three important studies have been published regarding the life and work of Ibn Sarabiyun, each of which dealing with a different aspect of the transmission of this important author’s œuvre. Likewise, during the last twenty-five years, a number of texts associated with Ibn Sarabiyun's works have been edited, allowing us today to shed new light on the relation between the original Syriac and the numerous translations into Arabic, Latin and Hebrew. Furthermore, through analysing and comparing a number of manuscripts containing different parts of Ibn Sarabiyun's work which have not hitherto been considered together, progress can be made towards answering the question how Ibn Sarabiyun was translated and used during the medieval period.

data.title: The Oriental Tradition of Paul of Aegina’s Pragmateia
data.abstractNote: The volume investigates how Paul of Aegina's medical handbook or pragmateia was transmitted and transformed through Syriac and Arabic translations, becoming one of the cornerstones of the Islamic medical tradition. It uses new manuscript evidence in order to explore the crucial impact of Paul's pragmateia, tracing its steps through different languages and cultures in the Middle East. A discussion of different Syriac and Arabic authors who quote the pragmateia such as Ibn Serapion and Rhazes is followed by detailed studies of Greek-Syriac-Arabic translation technique, examining, for instance, ophthalmologic terminology, and giving a critical appraisal of translation syntax and lexicography. Paul's influence on the development of medical theory in the Islamic world and beyond is also addressed, making it an important contribution not only to Graeco-Arabic studies, but also to the history of medicine in general.

data.title: Evidence of Greek Philosophical Concepts in the Writings of Ephrem the Syrian
data.abstractNote: The theology of Ephrem the Syrian (ca. 306-373) has often been described as unhellenized and arising out of a predominantly Semitic cultural environment. This evaluation is based partly on the fact that Ephrem wrote in Syriac, a dialect of the Aramaic language spoken by the earliest Christians, and partly on his poetic approach to theology, which illustrates each thought with an abundance of symbols and paradoxes. This evaluation is problematic, however, because it emphasizes language and form over content, and because it overlooks those elements of Ephrem's thought that originate from the Greek world. This dissertation demonstrates that Ephrem was familiar with a variety of Greek philosophical concepts; his theology can therefore no longer be described as Semitic and unhellenized. The first chapter of this study introduces Ephrem's cultural context, the cities of Nisibis and Edessa, and discusses the degree of Hellenization in late antique Mesopotamia. The second chapter examines Ephrem's attitude towards learning, and it suggests how Ephrem might have been educated. Chapter three discusses Ephrem's use of the expressions 'itya and 'ituta, kyana, and qnoma, and compares these terms to the corresponding Greek terminology. The following chapters analyze in detail Ephrem's notion of the four elements (chapter four), atomism (chapter five), space (chapter six), incorporeals (chapter seven), and sense perception (chapter eight), comparing Ephrem's notions with the corresponding concepts in the Greek philosophical literature. Chapter nine summarizes the results. The great number of parallels between Ephrem and Hellenic philosophers shows that he shared in the Greek cultural tradition to a larger extent than has usually been acknowledged. Ephrem self-consciously avails himself of Greek philosophy in order to refute his theological opponents. His occasional polemics against Greek philosophy occur exclusively in the context of his criticism of inappropriate investigation into the nature of the divine. Ephrem's use of Greek philosophy is predominantly Stoic, but also eclectic - like that of many other early theologians. Although the paucity of evidence concerning early Syriac culture does not permit drawing more than speculative conclusions about how the Greek traditions were conveyed to Ephrem, this dissertation shows that they were part of his intellectual heritage.

data.title: Expectations of the End in Early Syriac Christianity
data.abstractNote: Apocalyptic imagery was widespread in the Greek and Latin patristic literature but occurs relatively seldom in the early Syriac sources. This paper surveys the eschatologies of Bardaisan, the Odes of Solomon, and the Acts of Thomas and suggests specific theological, sociological, and historical reasons why apocalyptic motifs were not employed on a large scale. Bardaisan’s opposition to Marcion would have made him reluctant to draw on any type of dualistic imagery, and his social setting at the center, not at the margins of his community was not one that typically gave rise to apocalyptic discourse. The Odes’ joyful praise of salvation experienced already now leaves no room for looming disasters or cosmic battles. Only the Acts of Thomas contain one element found in apocalyptic literature: a tour of hell, which in the Acts serves a parenetic function. This paper also suggests that the scarcity of apocalyptic motifs in early Syriac Christianity can to some extent be attributed to the location of these Christians at the frontier.

data.title: Bardaisan and Origen on Fate and the Power of the Stars
data.abstractNote: Bardaisan of Edessa (d. 222) is one of the earliest theologians to reflect on the proper place of the heavenly bodies within a Christian cosmology. Bardaisan draws on both biblical texts and contemporary philosophical notions to argue that planets and stars are created by God and are subject to the divine commandment, yet are also endowed with a certain freedom on account of which they will be judged on the last day. Bardaisan, wishing to maintain the oneness and goodness of God against Marcionite dualism, regards the heavenly bodies as responsible for undesirable events that are beyond the control of human will or natural law. This paper compares and contrasts Bardaisan's understanding of fate and astral power with that of his younger contemporary Origen. It argues that Bardaisan's cosmology is not an isolated phenomenon at the margins of the Christian world, but is part of a larger trajectory of speculative thought within third-century Christianity.

data.title: Selbstverständnis und Bildungsauftrag der Schule von Nisibis
data.abstractNote: The School of Nisibis was a prominent center of Christian learning in the Sasanid Empire. It inspired the foundation of schools elsewhere in the Persian realm and also influenced intellectuals in the Graeco-Roman world. This article outlines the school’s history from the fifth through the early seventh century, highlights its contribution to church life and monasticism, and describes the life at the school based on the Statutes and other contemporary documents. Particular attention is given to the Preface of the Statutes, which reflects the community’s self-understanding in the early seventh century, a time when the school reconstituted itself after a divisive dispute surrounding its director Ḥenana. The article argues that the school should not be regarded as a kind of monastery (as has sometimes been suggested), but is better understood as an institution of Christian higher education. The school’s motivation ultimately was a theological one: to exemplify and contribute to the salvation historical process, which was envisioned as an ongoing process of learning, directed by God as divine pedagogue.

data.title: Transmitting Theodore to the Church of the East: The Contribution of Thomas of Edessa
data.abstractNote: Thomas of Edessa (d. c. 540), author of Explanations of the Nativity and of Epiphany, flourished as a teacher at the School of Nisibis in Sasanid Persia. By analysing his understanding of salvation history, exegesis and the idea of the human being as ‘bond of creation’, this article shows how Thomas took up and popularised concepts central to the theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia. The article posits that the Nisibene school theology of Thomas and others constituted – alongside liturgy, canonical decrees and biblical commentaries – one of the principal avenues by which Theodore's theology was transmitted to the Church of the East.

data.title: The Theological Significance of Analogy Language in the Teaching of Syriac Fathers and its Impact on Theology of Today
data.abstractNote: Like any other science theology has a specific language which should express and clarify its essentials. Because most of the subjects of theological research are immeasurable scientific language has to operate using images and theoretical terms. Of course there are many methodologies of theological discourse. Among them one can find the methodology developed by Church Fathers especially those belonging to both West and East Syriac Traditions. Since their mentality was close to the Semitic roots they started to use in the theological treatises a very specific kind of explanation which could be well understood by the people of Middle East. It was a language of analogy. Thanks to the use of tangible images the Fathers invented a direct language which enabled them to explain truths that could not be clarified using ordinary language. In this paper we try to explain the importance of analogy in theological debate. The explanation will be supported by some examples taken from the writings of the prominent Syriac Fathers regarding the baptismal analogies and the typology “Mary – Eve”, seen as an example of the theological explanation of the divine truth. In the final part of this study we attempt to outline the accommodation of analogical language to contemporary theological discussion and liturgical practice.
